claims.text: The Beyond the Imitation Game benchmark (BIG-bench) contains 204 tasks contributed across diverse topics.
Average language model performance on BIG-bench improves with compute scale and shot count, but best models achieve a normalized aggregate score below 20 compared to expert human raters.
Language model probability calibration improves consistently with increased scale on multiple-choice tasks.
BIG-G sparse models achieve a roughly twofold improvement in inference compute cost compared to dense models for equivalent BIG-bench aggregate performance.
BIG-G sparse models achieve approximately a tenfold improvement in FLOP-matched parameter count needed to reach a given calibration score compared to dense models.
Tasks with high performance linearity across model scales rely predominantly on knowledge memorization or simple text manipulations.
Tasks exhibiting sudden breakthrough behavior at critical scales are composite tasks requiring multiple discrete steps or distinct skills.
Including answer choices in the input query prompt reduces multiple-choice task performance across model scales compared to omitting choices from the prompt.
Model social bias increases with scale in task settings presenting broad or ambiguous contexts.
Model social bias decreases with scale in task settings with narrow, unambiguous contexts.
Few-shot prompting demonstrating neutrality significantly reduces model social bias on ambiguous tasks.
Evaluated language models perform substantially worse on non-English tasks than on English tasks, especially on low-resource languages.
In the checkmate-in-one chess task, the capability to propose legal chess moves improves smoothly with scale even though checkmate accuracy remains low.

evidence.description: BIG-bench currently consists of 204 tasks, contributed by 450 authors across 132 institutions.
In plots of aggregate performance, this normalized preferred metric is averaged over all tasks. The best performing language models achieved a score of less than 20, well below expert human baseline.
Figure 5 shows expected calibration error and Brier score across 109 multiple choice tasks, showing consistent calibration improvement with model scale.
BIG-G sparse models perform better on BIG-bench tasks than BIG-G dense models, achieving a roughly twofold improvement in inference cost for the same model performance.
Sparse models achieve about a tenfold improvement in the FLOP-matched parameter count needed to reach a given calibration score.
Tasks with highest linearity rely mostly on memorization of information that exists in training data, such as qa_wikidata, linguistic_mappings, and mult_data_wrangling.
Tasks that see strong breakthrough behavior include modified_arithmetic, repeat_copy_logic, and figure_of_speech_detection, which require applying several distinct skills or discrete steps.
Figure 10 demonstrates that including multiple choice options in input queries hurts performance across all shot counts compared to evaluation without appended choices.

Across six social bias tasks with broad/ambiguous contexts, aggregate bias scores decrease with scale; e.g., the 128B model finds it 22x more likely that a white boy will grow up to be a good doctor than a Native American girl.
Figure 13a shows bias decreasing with model size in unambiguously prompted bbq_lite_json subtasks.
Figure 13b shows that few-shot prompting indicating neutrality as the desired response significantly reduces model bias in ambiguous contexts.
While English entailed_polarity accuracy reaches 90% with scale, Hindi entailed_polarity shows no scaling trend and stays below 70% accuracy.
The 128B parameter model finds only 6 checkmates out of 1024 zero-shot examples, but its rate of outputting legal moves improves smoothly from near 0 to over 50%.

methodologies.name: BIG-bench Benchmark Suite
methodologies.description: A collaborative benchmark of 204+ JSON and programmatic Python tasks evaluated across transformer model classes and parameter scales.

methodologies.name: Human Expert Rater Baseline Evaluation
methodologies.description: Evaluation of benchmark tasks by human raters with access to external resources under timed daily evaluation sessions.
conditions: 30 to 120 minutes per day time constraint

limitations.text: Prior language modeling benchmarks suffer from narrow task scope, rapid performance saturation within 18 months, and noisy data labeling by non-experts.
Full evaluation on BIG-bench is computationally expensive, particularly for programmatic tasks that require multiple sequential model queries.
BIG-bench evaluates pure text language models and does not cover multi-modal capabilities.

Current language model architectures cannot integrate long context windows, lack episodic memory, cannot perform recurrent computation before token output, and cannot ground knowledge across physical modalities.
Human rater baselines are subject to variance from rater background, demographic representation, subsampling, and strict session time limits.

future_work.text: Extend language model benchmarking to cover multi-modal capabilities.
Investigate qualitative differences in capabilities and scaling behavior between sparse expert models and dense models.
Develop architectural and training interventions to resolve long-context integration, recurrent token-level computation, and multi-sensory grounding.
